::: {.callout-note}
**This chapter is about what changes when the data no longer fits on your laptop.**

**Assumed knowledge:** Sessions 2–3 — pandas, loading and cleaning. Nothing else.

**The one idea to take away:** "big data" is not a size, it is a **symptom**. It begins at
the point where one machine stops being enough — and that point arrives far later than
most people think. Every demo in this chapter runs on your laptop.
:::

## 🎯 Learning outcomes {#sec-s13-outcomes}

By the end of this chapter you can:

1. Explain the five Vs and say which one actually causes trouble in a given project.
2. Measure the point at which pandas starts to struggle on your own machine.
3. Process a file larger than memory using chunks.
4. Name the four types of analytics and give an example of each.
5. Explain how HDFS stores a file across many machines and survives a failure.
6. Place the main big-data tools on a map and say what each is for.
7. Say when **not** to use big-data tools.
8. Run a real chunked calculation on a dataset with over half a million rows.

# Part A — What makes data big {#sec-s13-a}

## 1. The five Vs {#sec-s13-topic-1}

**Big data is usually described with five words beginning with V.** They are useful as a
checklist, provided you remember that **only one of them is usually your actual problem.**

| V | Means | The problem it creates |
|---|---|---|
| **Volume** | how much there is | it does not fit in memory or on one disk |
| **Velocity** | how fast it arrives | you cannot store it before the next batch arrives |
| **Variety** | how many shapes it comes in | text, images, JSON and tables need different handling |
| **Veracity** | how much you can trust it | sensors fail, users lie, systems disagree |
| **Value** | whether it is worth anything | most of it is never used |

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — the library"}
**Volume** — the library has ten million books, and no room for shelves.
**Velocity** — twelve thousand new books arrive every hour.
**Variety** — some are books, some are scrolls, some are audio recordings.
**Veracity** — some are unreliable, and some are simply wrong.
**Value** — nine million of them will never be opened.

**A library with a volume problem needs a bigger building. One with a velocity problem
needs a faster door.** They are different problems with different solutions, and calling
both "big data" hides that.
:::

## 2. Where one machine stops being enough {#sec-s13-topic-2}

**The honest threshold is not a number of rows. It is the point where the work no longer
fits in memory.**

A rough guide: pandas comfortably handles data up to about **one fifth of your RAM**,
because operations make copies. Beyond that your machine starts swapping to disk and
everything slows by orders of magnitude.

### Demo 1 — measure it on your own machine

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import time

# Read one real file, then time the same operation on growing slices of it.
base = pd.read_csv("datasets/transactions.csv", usecols=["shop", "amount"])
big = pd.concat([base] * 20, ignore_index=True)      # 4 million rows from one file
print(f"source file: {len(base):,} rows; stacked to {len(big):,} for the largest test\n")

print(f"{'rows':>12} {'memory':>12} {'groupby time':>14} {'per M rows':>12}")
print("-" * 54)

for n in [10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000, 4_000_000]:
    df = big.iloc[:n]
    mem = df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6

    start = time.perf_counter()
    result = df.groupby("shop")["amount"].mean()
    secs = time.perf_counter() - start

    print(f"{n:>12,} {mem:>10.1f} MB {secs*1000:>12.1f} ms {secs/(n/1e6)*1000:>10.1f} ms")

print("\nThe cost per million rows stays roughly flat — pandas is not struggling yet.")
print("It struggles when the data plus its working copies stop fitting in RAM.")
```

### Demo 2 — how much memory a realistic table needs

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("datasets/transactions.csv", parse_dates=["ts"])
n = len(df)

per_row = df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / n
print(f"this table: {df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB for {n:,} rows "
      f"({per_row:.0f} bytes per row)\n")

print(f"{'rows':>16} {'estimated size':>16} {'fits in 16 GB RAM?'}")
for rows in [1e6, 1e7, 1e8, 1e9]:
    gb = rows * per_row / 1e9
    verdict = "yes, comfortably" if gb < 3 else "tight — use chunks" if gb < 16 else "NO — needs a cluster"
    print(f"{rows:>16,.0f} {gb:>13.1f} GB   {verdict}")
```

### Demo 3 — two ways to survive a file bigger than memory

**Before reaching for a cluster, two techniques solve most "too big" problems on one
machine.**

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, tempfile, os

path = "datasets/transactions.csv"
with open(path) as f:
    n = sum(1 for _ in f) - 1        # count data rows, excluding the header
print(f"file on disk: {os.path.getsize(path)/1e6:.1f} MB, {n:,} rows\n")

# --- TECHNIQUE 1: chunking. Never hold the whole file at once. -------------
running_total, running_count = 0.0, 0
per_city = {}
for chunk in pd.read_csv(path, chunksize=50_000):        # 50,000 rows at a time
    running_total += chunk["amount"].sum()
    running_count += len(chunk)
    for city, total in chunk.groupby("city")["amount"].sum().items():
        per_city[city] = per_city.get(city, 0) + total

per_city_rounded = {city: round(total) for city, total in per_city.items()}
print(f"CHUNKED: mean amount {running_total/running_count:.2f} over {running_count:,} rows")
print(f"         totals per city: {per_city_rounded}")
print(f"         peak memory held: one chunk of 50,000 rows, not {n:,}")

# --- TECHNIQUE 2: read only what you need ---------------------------------
narrow = pd.read_csv(path, usecols=["city", "amount"])
wide   = pd.read_csv(path)
print(f"\nCOLUMN SELECTION: all columns {wide.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB")
print(f"                  two columns  {narrow.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB")

# --- BONUS: the right dtype often halves the memory -----------------------
compact = wide.copy()
compact["city"] = compact["city"].astype("category")
compact["shop"] = compact["shop"].astype("int8")
print(f"\nDTYPES:  before {wide.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB"
      f"  →  after {compact.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB")
```

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Try these before you build a cluster"}
Chunking, selecting columns and fixing dtypes routinely turn a "we need Spark" problem
back into a laptop problem. **A distributed cluster costs money, expertise and
debugging time.** Spend a day on the three techniques above first — most of the time,
that is the whole solution.
:::

# Part B — Four types of analytics {#sec-s13-b}

## 3. The four questions {#sec-s13-topic-3}

**Every analysis is one of four kinds, in increasing order of difficulty and value.**

| Type | Question | Example | Covered in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Descriptive** | *What happened?* | sales fell 12% last quarter | Sessions 7–8 |
| **Diagnostic** | *Why did it happen?* | the fall was entirely in one region | Session 8 |
| **Predictive** | *What will happen?* | next quarter will fall another 5% | Sessions 9–11 |
| **Prescriptive** | *What should we do?* | move stock to the region that is growing | Session 16 |

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    D["<b>Descriptive</b><br/>what happened?"] --> G["<b>Diagnostic</b><br/>why?"]
    G --> P["<b>Predictive</b><br/>what next?"]
    P --> X["<b>Prescriptive</b><br/>what should we do?"]
```

### Demo 4 — all four on one dataset

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd

sales = pd.read_csv("datasets/regional_sales.csv", parse_dates=["month"])

# 1. DESCRIPTIVE — what happened?
by_month = sales.groupby("month")["sales"].sum()
change = (by_month.iloc[-1] - by_month.iloc[0]) / by_month.iloc[0]
print(f"DESCRIPTIVE : total sales moved {change:+.1%} across the year")

# 2. DIAGNOSTIC — why? Compute the change over the year, one region at a time.
change_by_region = {}
for region, group in sales.groupby("region"):
    group_sorted = group.sort_values("month")
    first_month = group_sorted["sales"].iloc[0]
    last_month = group_sorted["sales"].iloc[-1]
    change_by_region[region] = last_month - first_month
by_region = pd.Series(change_by_region)

print("DIAGNOSTIC  : change by region over the year")
for r, v in by_region.items():
    print(f"                {r:<6} {v:>+10,.0f}")
print(f"              → the decline is entirely {by_region.idxmin()}; the others grew")

# 3. PREDICTIVE — what next?
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
x = np.arange(len(by_month)).reshape(-1, 1)
trend_model = LinearRegression().fit(x, by_month.values)
next3 = trend_model.predict([[12], [13], [14]])
print(f"PREDICTIVE  : next three months ≈ {', '.join(f'{v:,.0f}' for v in next3)}")

# 4. PRESCRIPTIVE — what should we do?
growing = by_region[by_region > 0].index.tolist()
print(f"PRESCRIPTIVE: shift investment from {by_region.idxmin()} to {', '.join(growing)};")
print(f"              re-examine {by_region.idxmin()} before writing it off")
```

**Notice the increasing difficulty.** Descriptive is a `groupby`. Prescriptive needs a
prediction *and* a judgement about what to do with it — which is why the last one is
never fully automatic.

# Part C — Distributed storage {#sec-s13-c}

## 4. How HDFS works {#sec-s13-topic-4}

**HDFS — the Hadoop Distributed File System — stores one enormous file across many
ordinary machines, and keeps working when some of them fail.**

Three ideas do all the work:

| Idea | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Blocks** | the file is cut into fixed-size pieces, typically 128 MB |
| **Replication** | every block is stored on **three** different machines |
| **Write once** | files are appended to, never edited in the middle |

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    F["one 400 MB file"] --> B1["block 1<br/>128 MB"]
    F --> B2["block 2<br/>128 MB"]
    F --> B3["block 3<br/>128 MB"]
    F --> B4["block 4<br/>16 MB"]
    B1 --> N["<b>NameNode</b><br/>remembers which block<br/>is on which machine"]
    B2 --> N
    B3 --> N
    B4 --> N
    N --> D1["DataNode 1"]
    N --> D2["DataNode 2"]
    N --> D3["DataNode 3"]
```

The **NameNode** holds the index — which blocks make up which file, and where each copy
lives. The **DataNodes** hold the actual blocks. **The NameNode never touches the data
itself**, which is why one modest machine can index petabytes.

### Demo 5 — block splitting and replication, simulated

```{python}
import math

def plan_storage(file_gb, block_mb=128, replication=3, datanodes=6):
    blocks = math.ceil(file_gb * 1024 / block_mb)
    copies = blocks * replication
    print(f"file size        : {file_gb} GB")
    print(f"block size       : {block_mb} MB")
    print(f"blocks           : {blocks:,}")
    print(f"copies stored    : {blocks:,} × {replication} = {copies:,}")
    print(f"disk used        : {file_gb * replication} GB "
          f"({replication}× the file, the price of surviving failures)")
    print(f"blocks per node  : about {copies // datanodes:,} across {datanodes} machines")
    print(f"machines that can fail without data loss: {replication - 1}")

plan_storage(400)
```

### Demo 6 — why replication is worth 3× the disk

```{python}
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(75)
n_nodes, annual_failure_rate, trials = 200, 0.04, 20_000

for replication in [1, 2, 3]:
    lost = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        failed = rng.random(n_nodes) < annual_failure_rate
        # a block is lost only if every machine holding a copy fails
        holders = rng.choice(n_nodes, replication, replace=False)
        if failed[holders].all():
            lost += 1
    print(f"replication {replication}: chance a given block is lost in a year "
          f"= {lost/trials:.4%}")

print(f"\n(with {n_nodes} machines and a {annual_failure_rate:.0%} annual failure rate)")
print("Three copies turns near-certain annual data loss into a negligible risk.")
```

## 5. Talking to HDFS {#sec-s13-topic-5}

**HDFS commands look deliberately like ordinary shell commands.** These need a running
Hadoop cluster, so they are shown rather than executed here.

```bash
# List a directory in the cluster
hdfs dfs -ls /user/data/logs
# Found 1 items
# -rw-r--r--   3 hadoop supergroup  1099511627776 2024-01-01 12:00 /user/data/logs/clicks.csv
#              ↑
#        this 3 is the replication factor: every block exists on three machines

# Copy a local file INTO the cluster
hdfs dfs -put ./local_logs.csv /user/data/logs/

# Copy a file back OUT of the cluster
hdfs dfs -get /user/data/logs/clicks.csv ./downloaded.csv

# Peek at the first lines of a 1 TB file, without downloading it
hdfs dfs -cat /user/data/logs/clicks.csv | head -20

# How is this file actually laid out across the cluster?
hdfs fsck /user/data/logs/clicks.csv -files -blocks -locations
```

::: {.callout-important title="🔓 Running this yourself"}
You do not need a cluster to complete this course. Three options, easiest first:

| Option | What you get | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| **PySpark local mode** | everything in Session 14 except the `hdfs dfs` commands | `pip install pyspark`, needs Java 17 |
| **Docker** | a real single-node Hadoop, so `hdfs dfs` commands work | one `docker run` |
| **A hosted sandbox** | a full cluster in a browser | sign-up only |

**Every executable cell in this chapter and the next runs in local mode.** The `bash`
blocks above are reference — they are the commands you would type against a real
cluster.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ HDFS is terrible at small files"}
One 128 MB file uses one block and one entry in the NameNode's index. **A million 128-byte
files use a million entries** — and the NameNode keeps its index in memory. Small files
exhaust the cluster's index long before they exhaust its disks.

**The fix is always the same: combine small files into large ones before storing them.**
:::

### Demo 7 — one file size, by hand

```{python}
total_gb, avg_file_mb = 10_000, 256      # 10 TB, stored as 256 MB files
files = total_gb * 1024 / avg_file_mb
mem_gb = files * 150 * 2 / 1e9           # ~150 bytes of NameNode memory per file, per block
print(f"{total_gb:,} GB as {avg_file_mb} MB files → {files:,.0f} files")
print(f"NameNode index needed: {mem_gb:.4f} GB ({mem_gb*1000:.1f} MB)")
```

**40,000 files is nothing — 12 MB of index.** The next demo repeats this for much smaller
files and watches the index grow.

### Demo 8 — the same 10 TB, four different file sizes

```{python}
def namenode_pressure(total_gb, avg_file_mb):
    files = total_gb * 1024 / avg_file_mb
    # roughly 150 bytes of NameNode memory per file plus per block
    mem_gb = files * 150 * 2 / 1e9
    print(f"{total_gb:>6} GB as {avg_file_mb:>6.2f} MB files → {files:>12,.0f} files, "
          f"NameNode index ≈ {mem_gb:>7.2f} GB")

print("Same amount of data, different file sizes:")
for size in [256, 64, 1, 0.1]:
    namenode_pressure(10_000, size)
```

# Part D — The toolkit {#sec-s13-d}

## 6. What all the names are {#sec-s13-topic-6}

**The big-data ecosystem is a pile of names. Sorted by what they do, it is short.**

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    subgraph ING["Getting data in"]
        K["<b>Kafka</b><br/>streams of events"]
        S["<b>Sqoop / Flume</b><br/>bulk import"]
    end
    subgraph ST["Storing it"]
        H["<b>HDFS</b><br/>files across machines"]
        HB["<b>HBase / Cassandra</b><br/>fast lookups"]
    end
    subgraph PR["Processing it"]
        MR["<b>MapReduce</b><br/>the original, disk-based"]
        SP["<b>Spark</b><br/>the successor, in memory"]
    end
    subgraph QU["Querying it"]
        HV["<b>Hive</b><br/>SQL over big files"]
        SS["<b>Spark SQL</b>"]
    end
    ING --> ST --> PR --> QU
```

| Tool | One sentence | Session |
|---|---|---|
| **HDFS** | stores files across many machines | this one |
| **YARN** | decides which machine runs which job | this one |
| **MapReduce** | the original processing model — simple, and slow | 14 |
| **Spark** | the successor — same idea, kept in memory, far faster | 14 |
| **Hive** | lets you write SQL against files in HDFS | 14 |
| **Kafka** | carries continuous streams of events | mentioned only |
| **HBase / Cassandra** | databases for fast lookups at scale | 15 |
| **MongoDB** | a document database for flexible records | 15 |

## 7. When not to use any of this {#sec-s13-topic-7}

**Distributed tools have a fixed overhead. Below a certain size they are slower than
pandas, not faster.**

### Demo 9 — the fixed cost, on its own

**Before modelling a whole crossover curve, look at just the fixed cost in isolation: a
cluster takes seconds to even start, no matter how small the job is.**

```{python}
import pandas as pd, time

base = pd.read_csv("datasets/transactions.csv", usecols=["shop", "amount"])

t0 = time.perf_counter()
base.groupby("shop")["amount"].mean()
laptop_s = time.perf_counter() - t0

cluster_startup_s = 8.0   # a real Spark session takes seconds just to start
print(f"laptop, {len(base):,} rows: {laptop_s*1000:.1f} ms")
print(f"a cluster's startup alone: {cluster_startup_s:.0f} s = {cluster_startup_s*1000:,.0f} ms")
print(f"the laptop finishes {cluster_startup_s/laptop_s:,.0f}x before the cluster has even started")
```

The exact multiple varies a little between runs, but it is always in the thousands — a
200,000-row `groupby` is over before a cluster has finished saying hello. The next demo
turns this into a full crossover curve across dataset sizes.

### Demo 10 — the overhead, quantified

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, time

CLUSTER_STARTUP_S = 8.0        # a real Spark session takes seconds to start
PER_TASK_OVERHEAD = 0.15       # scheduling, serialising, shuffling

base = pd.read_csv("datasets/transactions.csv", usecols=["shop", "amount"])
big = pd.concat([base] * 25, ignore_index=True)

print(f"{'rows':>12} {'pandas':>10} {'distributed (modelled)':>24}   winner")
print("-" * 62)
for n in [10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000, 5_000_000]:
    df = big.iloc[:n]

    t = time.perf_counter()
    df.groupby("shop")["amount"].mean()
    pandas_s = time.perf_counter() - t

    # A cluster splits the work but pays startup and coordination costs.
    partitions = max(4, n // 250_000)
    dist_s = CLUSTER_STARTUP_S + PER_TASK_OVERHEAD * partitions + (pandas_s / 8)

    winner = "pandas" if pandas_s < dist_s else "distributed"
    print(f"{n:>12,} {pandas_s*1000:>8.1f} ms {dist_s*1000:>21,.0f} ms   {winner}")

print("\nThe modelled cluster never wins here, because none of these datasets is")
print("large enough to repay an 8-second startup. That crossover is the number")
print("you must find for yourself — Session 14 measures it with real Spark.")
```

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ 'Big data' is a claim that needs evidence"}
Before adopting distributed tooling, answer three questions with numbers:

1. **How large is the data actually?** — in GB, measured, not estimated
2. **Have I tried chunking, column selection and dtypes?** — Demo 3
3. **How long does the job take now, and how long is acceptable?**

If the answer to 3 is "four minutes, and ten would be fine", **you do not have a big-data
problem.** You have a four-minute job.
:::


# Part E — On a real file {#sec-s13-e}

## 8. The same three ideas, on 566,602 real rows {#sec-s13-topic-8}

**Every demo so far has run on data built for the lesson. Here is one built from a real
file, so you can see the same ideas hold up outside a made-up example.**

The file is `covertype.csv` — 566,602 real measurements of forest terrain from the US
Forest Service, published on Hugging Face
([`inria-soda/tabular-benchmark`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/inria-soda/tabular-benchmark)).
Ten numeric columns describe a patch of land; `Y` says whether it is one particular kind
of forest cover or not. Get it once with:

```bash
python datasets/download_bigdata_real.py
```

### Demo 11 — load it whole, then load it in chunks, and compare

```{python}
import pandas as pd, numpy as np, time, os

path = "datasets/bigdata/covertype.csv"
print(f"file on disk: {os.path.getsize(path)/1e6:.1f} MB\n")

# --- THE WHOLE FILE AT ONCE ------------------------------------------------
t0 = time.perf_counter()
whole = pd.read_csv(path)
load_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
whole_mb = whole.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6
print(f"whole file : {len(whole):,} rows, loaded in {load_s:.2f}s, "
      f"held {whole_mb:.1f} MB in memory")

t0 = time.perf_counter()
answer_whole = whole.groupby("Y")[["X1", "X2", "X3"]].mean()
print(f"groupby    : {time.perf_counter()-t0:.3f}s\n")
print(answer_whole)

# --- THE SAME QUESTION, ONE CHUNK OF 50,000 ROWS AT A TIME -----------------
t0 = time.perf_counter()
totals = {0: np.zeros(3), 1: np.zeros(3)}
counts = {0: 0, 1: 0}
peak_chunk_mb = 0.0

for chunk in pd.read_csv(path, usecols=["X1", "X2", "X3", "Y"], chunksize=50_000):
    peak_chunk_mb = max(peak_chunk_mb, chunk.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6)
    for y, group in chunk.groupby("Y"):
        totals[y] += group[["X1", "X2", "X3"]].sum().values
        counts[y] += len(group)

chunk_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"\nchunked    : {chunk_s:.2f}s, the biggest single chunk held only "
      f"{peak_chunk_mb:.2f} MB")
for y in (0, 1):
    print(f"  Y={y}: mean = {(totals[y] / counts[y]).round(4)}   n={counts[y]:,}")

print(f"\nsame answer, {whole_mb/peak_chunk_mb:.0f}x less memory at any one moment")
```

**The numbers match to four decimal places, and the chunked version never held more than
a few megabytes at once.** This is Demo 3's lesson — chunk it, do not hold it all — proven
on a file with over half a million real rows instead of a file built to make the point.

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 What changed, going from the toy demo to the real file"}
Nothing in the code changed in kind — only in scale. The same `chunksize=` argument, the
same running totals, the same reason for doing it. **That is the whole point of this
section**: the techniques in this chapter are not toy tricks that stop working on real
data. They are the same three lines, run on a bigger file.
:::

# 🎯 Tasks {#sec-s13-tasks}

::: {.callout-note title="✏️ Practise"}
**Task 1 — Find your own limit.** Extend Demo 1 to 10 and 20 million rows. **Report the
row count at which the time per million rows starts to rise**, and how much RAM your
machine has.

**Task 2 — Chunk a real job.** Using the chunking pattern from Demo 3, compute the
**median** amount per city. **Explain why this is harder than the mean** and what you did
about it.

**Task 3 — Classify the questions.** Which of the four types: "which products are most
often returned?"; "will this customer return this item?"; "why did returns rise in
March?"; "which items should we stop stocking?"

**Task 4 — Size a cluster.** You have 8 TB of logs, a 128 MB block size and replication
3. **Report the number of blocks, the total disk needed, and how many 4 TB machines you
would buy.**
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
```{python}
import math, numpy as np, pandas as pd

print("Task 2 — the mean can be computed from running totals, so chunks combine")
print("  trivially. The median cannot: you need all the values for a city at once,")
print("  or an approximation. Two workable approaches:")
print("    a) collect just the one column per city across chunks, then take the median")
print("    b) use an approximate quantile from a histogram built chunk by chunk")

print("\nTask 3")
for q, kind in [("which products are most often returned?", "DESCRIPTIVE"),
                ("will this customer return this item?",    "PREDICTIVE"),
                ("why did returns rise in March?",          "DIAGNOSTIC"),
                ("which items should we stop stocking?",    "PRESCRIPTIVE")]:
    print(f"  {q:<44} {kind}")

# Task 4
tb, block_mb, rep, disk_per_node_tb = 8, 128, 3, 4
blocks = math.ceil(tb * 1024 * 1024 / block_mb)
total_tb = tb * rep
print(f"\nTask 4 — {blocks:,} blocks; {total_tb} TB of disk needed;")
print(f"         {math.ceil(total_tb / disk_per_node_tb)} machines at {disk_per_node_tb} TB each,")
print(f"         and in practice more, since you never fill a cluster to 100%.")
```
::::

# ❓ MCQs {#sec-s13-mcqs}

**Q1.** A hospital receives 50,000 sensor readings per second and must react within a
second. Which V is the problem?

- (a) Volume.
- (b) **Velocity.**
- (c) Value.

**Q2.** A 40 GB CSV must be summarised on a laptop with 16 GB of RAM. What do you try
first?

- (a) Buy a cluster.
- (b) **Read it in chunks and select only the needed columns.**
- (c) Sample 1% and hope.

**Q3.** "Sales fell because the North region lost its two largest customers." Which type?

- (a) Descriptive.
- (b) **Diagnostic.**
- (c) Prescriptive.

**Q4.** HDFS replicates every block three times. What does that cost and buy?

- (a) Costs nothing, buys speed.
- (b) **Costs 3× the disk, buys survival when up to two machines holding a block fail.**
- (c) Costs 3× the time, buys accuracy.

**Q5.** Your cluster has plenty of disk free but the NameNode is out of memory. Likely
cause?

- (a) A single enormous file.
- (b) **Millions of tiny files, each needing an index entry.**
- (c) Replication set too low.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"}
**A1 — (b).** The total volume may be modest; the difficulty is the rate and the deadline.

**A2 — (b).** Demo 3. Chunking plus column selection solves most of these.

**A3 — (b).** It explains *why*, which is the diagnostic question.

**A4 — (b).** Demo 6 measured the failure probabilities.

**A5 — (b).** The small-files problem — the NameNode's index lives in memory.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="✅ Before you move on"}
- [ ] I can name the five Vs and say which one a given project actually suffers from
- [ ] I have measured where pandas starts to struggle on my own machine
- [ ] I can process a file larger than memory using chunks
- [ ] I can explain blocks, replication and the NameNode
- [ ] I know why HDFS hates small files
- [ ] **Easiest thing to forget:** try chunking, column selection and dtypes before
      reaching for a cluster. They usually turn the problem back into a laptop problem.
:::
